profile.name: Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library
profile.tagline: Inspiring leadership, conservation, and courageous citizenship through the life and legacy of Theodore Roosevelt.

items.headline: The Panama Canal: Roosevelt's Bold Gambit for American Power

items.headline: The Brownsville Affair: An Injustice That Took 66 Years to Correct
items.blurb: In 1906, soldiers of the all-Black 25th Infantry were wrongly accused after a Brownsville, Texas shooting, an injustice not corrected for 66 years.

items.headline: Ethel Roosevelt Derby: The Devoted Daughter
items.blurb: Steady and principled, Ethel Roosevelt Derby grew up at Sagamore Hill as Theodore and Edith's most grounded and devoted daughter.

items.headline: Maltese Cross Ranch: Roosevelt's Dakota Foothold
items.blurb: Seven miles south of Medora on the Little Missouri, the Maltese Cross Ranch was Roosevelt's first tangible commitment to the Dakota frontier.

items.headline: Trust-Busting: Roosevelt's War on Monopoly
items.blurb: In 1902, Roosevelt's government sued the Northern Securities railroad monopoly under the Sherman Antitrust Act, asserting bold new presidential power.

items.headline: The Rough Riders: America's Most Famous Regiment
items.blurb: Roosevelt and Wood recruited over 1,000 cowboys, Ivy League athletes, miners, and lawmen into the 1st Volunteer Cavalry, the famed Rough Riders.

items.blurb: The Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library and Museum masterfully harmonizes history, nature, and technology.

items.headline: The Adventure of the Three Boat Thieves: Justice on the Little Missouri
items.blurb: When three men stole his boat in March 1886, Roosevelt chased them down the icy Little Missouri to uphold the rule of law in the Badlands.

items.headline: Downward Bull Moose: Yoga with T.R.
51 Federal Bird Reserves: Roosevelt's Ornithological Vision
items.blurb: A boyhood love of birds led Theodore Roosevelt to establish 51 federal bird reserves, pioneering federal protection for America's wildlife.

items.headline: Lesson #37: To know a leader, know who they listen to
items.blurb: Edith Roosevelt's influence didn't come from a title — it came from being listened to.

items.headline: Lesson #36: An ever more perfect union requires an ever wider “we”
items.blurb: TR widened the circle of "We the People" further than almost any president before him — conservation, reform, the conviction that everybody counts.
